sheet.howExamined: P2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed, no formula sheet. The usual forms are a table to complete in order of wavelength, [1] per cell (Summer 2022 and 2025), a line from each of four waves to its danger [4] (Summer 2022 and 2025), sentences to complete (Summer 2023) and questions about only the regions listed (Summer 2021). Higher Tier adds a v = f λ calculation with the speed of light in standard form. The topic carried the paper's 6-mark banded question at both tiers in Summer 2024.
traps: Swapping the two ends of the spectrum, radio and gamma (Summer 2024 P2 F Q5 and P2 H Q2)

Writing ultrasound where ultraviolet is meant (Summer 2025 P2 F Q2)
Confusing the heating effects of microwaves and infrared (Summer 2023 P2 F Q3)
Not knowing that hot objects emit infrared (Summer 2024 P2 F Q5)
Forgetting that the colours travel at different speeds in glass, while every region shares one speed in a vacuum (Summer 2025 P2 H Q8, Summer 2023 P2 F Q7)
Reading a question about wavelength order as if it asked for frequency order
Multiplying instead of dividing when rearranging v = f λ

noteBlocks.lede: Sunlight on your face, a radio in the kitchen, a phone finding a signal, an X-ray at the dentist. They are one family of wave stretched to very different lengths, and the family runs in a fixed order.
can: Name the seven regions in order, in either direction

noteBlocks.md: Sunlight warming your face, a phone finding a signal, a dentist taking an X-ray. Those are all the same kind of wave, stretched to very different lengths. Together they make one family, and the family runs in a fixed order.

noteBlocks.caption: Seven regions, one ladder. Learn it one way and read it backwards when a question needs the other.

noteBlocks.md: Reading down the ladder, the **wavelength gets shorter** and the **frequency gets higher**: **radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays**. Say the order aloud until it sticks. Nearly every question on this topic asks you to place a region, or to compare two of them, and the ladder answers both.

noteBlocks.stem: Put these regions in order of increasing frequency: X-rays, microwaves, visible light, radio waves. [2]

steps.working: Increasing frequency starts at the low end: radio waves first.
steps.decision: Decide which way the list runs before you place anything.

steps.working: Microwaves come next, then visible light further along.
steps.decision: Walk down the ladder, keeping only the regions the question names.

steps.working: X-rays last: they sit near the high-frequency end.
steps.decision: Only gamma rays are higher, and they are not in this list.

noteBlocks.finalAnswer: radio waves, microwaves, visible light, X-rays

noteBlocks.prompt: In order of increasing frequency, which region comes straight after microwaves?
noteBlocks.explain: Walk down the ladder from the low-frequency end, as the See it did: radio waves, microwaves, then infrared, before visible light. So infrared comes straight after microwaves.

optionNotes.why: Visible light is one rung further on: infrared sits between microwaves and visible light.
Radio waves come before microwaves, at the low-frequency end; the question asks what comes after.

twin.prompt: In order of increasing frequency, which region comes straight after ultraviolet?
twin.explain: After ultraviolet the ladder runs X-rays, then gamma rays at the very end. So X-rays come straight after ultraviolet.

optionNotes.why: Gamma rays are at the very end of the spectrum, one rung past X-rays; straight after ultraviolet comes X-rays.
Visible light comes before ultraviolet in order of increasing frequency, not after it: the order runs visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays.

noteBlocks.alt: Radio waves, visible light and gamma rays drawn with very different wavelengths between a start line and a finish line; each travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum.
noteBlocks.caption: Different wavelengths, different frequencies, one speed in a vacuum.

noteBlocks.md: Two things never change across the family. Every region is a **transverse** wave, and in a **vacuum** every region travels at the **same speed**, 3 × 10⁸ m/s. A gamma ray is not faster than a radio wave; it simply fits far more waves into each second.

noteBlocks.title: Why the regions form one spectrum
noteBlocks.md: The speed is fixed, so wavelength and frequency are locked together: when one doubles, the other halves. That is v = f λ with v unable to change. The seven regions are one continuous range, cut into seven named pieces.

noteBlocks.stem: Radio waves from a spacecraft and X-rays from the Sun both cross the vacuum of space. Compare their speeds, their wavelengths and their frequencies. [3]

steps.decision: Both are electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, and every region travels at that one speed.

steps.working: Wavelength: the radio waves' is far longer.
steps.decision: Radio waves sit at the long-wavelength end of the ladder, X-rays near the other end.

steps.working: Frequency: the X-rays' is far higher.
steps.decision: At one fixed speed a shorter wavelength means more waves each second: v = f λ.

noteBlocks.prompt: A radio signal and a gamma ray leave the same star at the same moment. Which reaches the Earth first?
options: the gamma ray, because its frequency is higher
the radio signal, because its wavelength is longer
noteBlocks.explain: In a vacuum every electromagnetic wave has the same speed, 3 × 10⁸ m/s, as step 1 of the See it says. The two cover the same distance at the same speed, so they arrive together. A higher frequency packs more waves into each second; it does not make the wave faster.

optionNotes.option: the gamma ray, because its frequency is higher
optionNotes.why: A higher frequency means more waves each second, not a faster wave: in a vacuum every region has the same speed.

optionNotes.option: the radio signal, because its wavelength is longer
optionNotes.why: Longer waves are not faster ones: in a vacuum radio waves and gamma rays share one speed, 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

twin.prompt: Microwaves and ultraviolet both cross the vacuum of space. How does the speed of the ultraviolet compare with the speed of the microwaves?
options: faster, because its frequency is higher
slower, because its wavelength is shorter
twin.explain: Both are electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, and every region travels there at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. A different frequency or wavelength does not change that speed.

optionNotes.option: faster, because its frequency is higher
optionNotes.why: A higher frequency means more waves each second, not a faster wave: in a vacuum every region travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

optionNotes.option: slower, because its wavelength is shorter
optionNotes.why: A shorter wavelength does not make a wave slower: in a vacuum ultraviolet and microwaves share one speed.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which two quantities change as you move along the electromagnetic spectrum, and which one does not?
options: wavelength and frequency change; the speed in a vacuum does not
wavelength and speed change; the frequency does not
frequency and speed change; the wavelength does not
noteBlocks.answer: wavelength and frequency change; the speed in a vacuum does not
noteBlocks.explain: Steps 2 and 3 of the See it compared the wavelength and the frequency, and both differ from region to region; step 1 found the speed the same. So wavelength and frequency change, and the speed in a vacuum does not.

optionNotes.option: wavelength and speed change; the frequency does not
optionNotes.why: The speed is the one thing fixed in a vacuum; the frequency changes along the ladder together with the wavelength.

optionNotes.option: frequency and speed change; the wavelength does not
optionNotes.why: The speed is the one thing fixed in a vacuum; the wavelength changes along the ladder together with the frequency.

twin.prompt: Moving from infrared to ultraviolet along the spectrum, what happens to the speed in a vacuum?
twin.explain: Every region travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. Moving along the spectrum changes the wavelength and the frequency, never that speed.

optionNotes.why: The frequency increases from infrared to ultraviolet, but the speed in a vacuum does not: every region travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
The wavelength decreases from infrared to ultraviolet, but the speed in a vacuum stays fixed at 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

noteBlocks.title: One equation, not printed
noteBlocks.md: **v = f λ**, and for any electromagnetic wave in a vacuum v is 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Rearranged: λ = v ÷ f and f = v ÷ λ. P2 prints no equations, so write it from memory, first: the equation earns the first mark, the substitution the second and the answer the third.

noteBlocks.stem: A radar transmitter works at a frequency of 1.5 × 10¹⁰ Hz. Radio waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the wavelength of its waves. [3]

steps.decision: The equation first, from memory.
Substitute the speed of light and the frequency, keeping the powers of ten.
Divide, keying the powers of ten with the calculator's exponent button, and give the unit.
A check: microwaves are centimetres long, so the size is believable.

noteBlocks.prompt: A microwave transmitter works at 3 × 10⁹ Hz. Calculate its wavelength, in m.
noteBlocks.explain: As in the See it: v = f λ, so λ = v ÷ f = (3 × 10⁸) ÷ (3 × 10⁹) = 0.1 m. Dividing by the frequency gives the wavelength; multiplying the two gives a number far too large to be a length.

twin.prompt: A mobile phone signal has a frequency of 1.5 × 10⁹ Hz. Calculate its wavelength, in m.

noteBlocks.md: Too much of any region can harm you, and the higher the frequency, the more damage it is likely to do. **Microwaves** heat body tissues internally. **Infrared** is felt as heat and burns the skin. **Ultraviolet** damages skin cells and can lead to skin cancer. **Intense visible light** damages the eyes. **X-rays and gamma rays** damage cells, which may lead to cancer.

noteBlocks.alt: A thermal camera image of a dog. The warmest parts, its eyes, nose and the inside of its ears, appear brightest, while the thick fur over its body appears much darker because less infrared escapes through it.
noteBlocks.caption: A thermal camera sees no visible light at all. Everything in this picture is infrared, and the brightest parts are the warmest.
noteBlocks.prompt: The nose and the inside of the ears are brightest, the thick fur is darkest. Say what that tells you about which objects emit infrared, and give the danger of too much infrared falling on your skin.

noteBlocks.title: Heating is not enough
noteBlocks.md: Summer 2025 Higher examiners found some answers giving heating as the microwave danger, but only the very best tied it to the tissue or organs inside the body. Name the part of the body in every danger: inside for microwaves, the skin for infrared, skin cells for ultraviolet, the eyes, and cells for X-rays and gamma rays.

noteBlocks.stem: State the danger of overexposure to each of these: intense visible light, X-rays, gamma rays. [3]

steps.working: Intense visible light: damages the eyes.
steps.decision: The eye is the organ that takes in visible light, so the eye is the part harmed: name it.

steps.working: X-rays: damage cells, which may lead to cancer.
steps.decision: A far higher frequency: the rays pass into the body and harm the cells themselves, so name the cells.

steps.working: Gamma rays: damage cells, which may lead to cancer, and are the most harmful of the three.
steps.decision: The same harm as X-rays, but the highest frequency of all, so the damage is most likely.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Physics Revision "Electromagnetic Waves"
noteBlocks.why: Freesciencelessons runs the whole spectrum end to end beside our own steps. It also gives a use for each region, which the CCEA specification does not examine: learn the dangers.

noteBlocks.prompt: An engineer works beside a powerful microwave transmitter that has been left switched on. What harm is overexposure most likely to do?
options: burns to the surface of the skin
noteBlocks.explain: Microwaves pass into the body and are absorbed by the tissue there, so they heat it from inside. As the See it did, name the part harmed: internal heating of body tissues. The word internal is what the mark needs.

optionNotes.option: burns to the surface of the skin
optionNotes.why: Surface burns belong to infrared, which the skin absorbs; microwaves go deeper and heat tissue inside the body.
Eye damage is the danger of intense visible light, not of microwaves.

twin.prompt: A sunbed gives out ultraviolet. What harm can overexposure to ultraviolet do?
options: damage to skin cells that can lead to skin cancer
twin.answer: damage to skin cells that can lead to skin cancer
twin.explain: Ultraviolet damages skin cells, which can lead to skin cancer. Internal heating is the microwave danger.

optionNotes.why: Internal heating is the microwave danger: microwaves pass into the body. Ultraviolet is taken in by the skin's surface cells.
Ultraviolet can harm the eyes too, but 'only' leaves out its main danger: damage to skin cells that can lead to skin cancer.

noteBlocks.md: **Which way does the table run?** A table of regions can run in order of decreasing wavelength (Summer 2022 Foundation) or increasing wavelength (Summer 2025 Foundation). Read its arrow before you fill a gap.
**Only the regions listed.** A question can list five regions and ask which of those has the largest wavelength (Summer 2021 Foundation). The answer is the longest of the list, not radio waves.
**Four waves, four dangers.** Link each wave to its danger with one line each (Summer 2022 and 2025). For microwaves the line must reach internal body tissue (Summer 2025 Higher).

noteBlocks.stem: Of the regions X-rays, microwaves, ultraviolet and visible light, which has the longest wavelength, and which the highest frequency? [2]

steps.working: Only the four listed count, not the whole spectrum.
steps.decision: Radio waves and gamma rays are not in the list, so neither can be an answer.

steps.working: In ladder order: microwaves, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays.
steps.decision: Place just the listed regions, top to bottom.
The top of the listed four.
The bottom of the listed four.

noteBlocks.prompt: Of infrared, ultraviolet and visible light, which has the longest wavelength?
noteBlocks.explain: Place only the three listed, as the See it did: infrared, visible light, ultraviolet from the top of the ladder down. The longest wavelength of these is infrared. Radio waves are longer still, but they are not in the list.

optionNotes.why: Radio waves have the longest wavelength of the whole spectrum, but the question asks only about the three regions it lists.
Ultraviolet sits past visible light towards gamma rays, so it has the shortest wavelength of the three, not the longest.

twin.prompt: Of radio waves, microwaves and visible light, which has the highest frequency?
twin.explain: Of the three listed, visible light sits lowest on the ladder, so it has the highest frequency. Gamma rays are higher still, but they are not in the list; radio waves have the lowest frequency of all.

optionNotes.why: Gamma rays have the highest frequency of the whole spectrum, but the question asks only about the three regions it lists.
Radio waves are at the other end of the spectrum: the lowest frequency of all, so the lowest of the three listed.

noteBlocks.md:
Put the seven regions in order, either way round.
Say what all seven share: transverse, and one speed in a vacuum.
Work out a wavelength or a frequency with v = f λ and 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
Give the danger of each region, naming the part of the body.

Expect a table to complete, a line from each wave to its danger, a sentence to finish, or the six-mark account of the spectrum, with a v = f λ calculation at Higher. Read the direction of any table, and answer from the regions listed. Stuck? Write the ladder down the margin first.

workedExamples.stem:
A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of $1 \times 10^{8}$ Hz. Radio waves travel at $3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s.
Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves. [4]

steps.decision: The same wave equation works for every electromagnetic wave. Write it down first: the paper prints no equations, and the equation line carries its own mark.
Rearrange before substituting, so the numbers only ever go into a finished equation.

options: Because the wavelength is the unknown, so it has to be on its own
Because dividing always gives a smaller answer
Because the speed is bigger than the frequency
whyMenu.explain: Rearranging is about which quantity you are looking for, not about which numbers happen to be bigger. Get λ alone, then substitute.

steps.decision: Bracket each standard-form number, or key each with the calculator's exponent button, so the whole of 1 × 10⁸ divides.
Finish with the unit. A check: radio waves are metres long, which is why radio aerials are the size they are.

twin.stem:
Green light has a frequency of $5 \times 10^{14}$ Hz. It travels at $3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s.
Calculate its wavelength. [4]

items.stem: Before we start, from the last topic: which family does a radio wave belong to?

options.feedback: Every electromagnetic wave is transverse, and radio waves are electromagnetic.
Only sound and ultrasound are longitudinal. If this is new, the waves topic covers it first.

items.stem: In the equation v = f λ, which quantity is v?

options.feedback: Speed in m/s, frequency in Hz, wavelength in m.
The wavelength is λ. If the equation is new, the waves topic sets it up.
The frequency is f. If the equation is new, the waves topic sets it up.

items.stem: Which unit is a frequency measured in?

options.feedback: Hertz: one hertz means one wave each second.
Metres measure a wavelength. Frequency counts waves per second, in hertz.
Seconds measure a period. Frequency is its reciprocal, measured in hertz.

items.stem: Which list gives the regions in order of increasing frequency?

options.text: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, …
options.feedback: Radio waves have the lowest frequency; the list climbs from there to gamma rays.

options.text: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, …
options.feedback: That is increasing wavelength, which runs the opposite way. Summer 2024 examiners named swapping the two ends as the common error.

options.text: visible light, radio waves, gamma rays, infrared, …
options.feedback: The regions are jumbled. Learn the order once, in one direction, and reverse it when a question asks for wavelength.

items.stem: Which danger does the specification give for microwaves?

options.feedback: Internal is the word that earns the mark: the heating happens inside the body, not on the skin.

options.text: burning the surface of the skin
options.feedback: That is the infrared danger. Summer 2023 examiners reported the heating effects of microwaves and infrared being swapped.
Heating alone was not credited. Summer 2025 examiners wanted the heating linked to internal body tissue or organs.

options.text: damaging skin cells and causing skin cancer
options.feedback: That is the ultraviolet danger. Each region on the specification has its own.

items.stem: What do all seven regions have in common when travelling through a vacuum?
items.skill: The same speed in a vacuum

options.text: they all travel at the same speed
options.feedback: All of them travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, whatever their wavelength.

options.text: the higher the frequency, the faster they travel
options.feedback: Speed does not depend on frequency in a vacuum. Different speeds for different colours happen inside glass, which is what makes a spectrum from a prism.

options.text: they all have the same wavelength
options.feedback: Wavelength is exactly what changes from one region to the next. The speed is what stays the same.

items.stem: Which of these emits infrared radiation?

options.feedback: Any object above absolute zero emits infrared, and the hotter it is the more it emits.

options.text: only objects hot enough to glow
options.feedback: Glowing means visible light. Infrared comes off long before an object is hot enough to glow, which is how a thermal camera sees in the dark.

options.text: only objects plugged into the mains
options.feedback: Emitting infrared has nothing to do with electricity. It depends on temperature. Summer 2024 examiners reported candidates unaware that hot objects emit infrared.

context.setting: Placing three regions from their position in the order

parts.stem: Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum that lies between infrared and ultraviolet.

scheme.examinerNote: The seven named regions are the only acceptable answers.

hints: It is the only region you can see.
parts.workedSolution: Visible light. Working up in frequency the order runs infrared, visible light, ultraviolet.

parts.stem: Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum with the longest wavelength.

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2024 examiners reported the two ends of the spectrum being swapped.

hints: Longest wavelength means lowest frequency, which is one end of the strip.
parts.workedSolution: Radio waves. They sit at the long-wavelength, low-frequency end of the spectrum.

commonErrors.feedback: The two ends have been swapped. Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and the highest frequency; radio waves have the longest wavelength. Summer 2024 examiners named mixing up these two extremes as the common error.

parts.stem: Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum with the highest frequency.
hints: Highest frequency is the other end of the strip from radio waves.
parts.workedSolution: Gamma rays. Highest frequency also means shortest wavelength and the most damage to cells.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the other end. Radio waves have the lowest frequency of the seven; gamma rays have the highest.

context.setting: Rebuilding the spectrum strip from a shuffled set of labels

parts.stem: Arrange the seven regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing wavelength, starting with the shortest.

scheme.for: all seven in the order gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves [2]; five or six in the right place [1]
scheme.examinerNote: Increasing wavelength runs the opposite way from increasing frequency; read the question.

hints: Shortest wavelength is the same end as highest frequency.
Say the order you know out loud, then write it backwards.
parts.workedSolution: Increasing wavelength means starting at the high-frequency end: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. That is the order you already know for increasing frequency, reversed.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the order of increasing frequency, which runs the other way. The question asks for increasing wavelength, so gamma rays come first and radio waves last.

emphasis: dangers as the specification lists them

context.setting: A safety notice for a school physics laboratory

parts.stem: State how overexposure to microwaves can harm the human body.

any: heat the water in your body
heat up the water in your body
tissues inside the body are heated
tissue inside the body is heated

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 examiners credited heating only when it was linked to internal body tissue or organs.

hints: Heating on its own is not enough. Where does the heating happen?
parts.workedSolution: Microwaves cause internal heating of body tissues: they are absorbed by water inside the body, so the heating happens under the skin rather than on it.

commonErrors.feedback: Heating is the right idea but not yet the right answer. Summer 2025 examiners credited only the candidates who linked the heating to internal body tissue or organs. Skin burns belong to infrared.

parts.stem: State how overexposure to ultraviolet radiation can harm the human body.

accepted: it damages skin cells and can lead to skin cancer

scheme.for: damages skin cells / can lead to skin cancer

hints: It is the reason sun cream exists.
parts.workedSolution: Certain wavelengths of ultraviolet damage skin cells, which can lead to skin cancer.

parts.stem: State how overexposure to infrared radiation can harm the human body.

accepted: it is felt as heat and burns the skin

scheme.for: felt as heat; causes skin burns
scheme.examinerNote: Infrared burns the surface; microwaves heat internally. Summer 2023 examiners reported the two being confused.

hints: Think about standing too close to a very hot fire.
parts.workedSolution: Infrared radiation is felt as heat and causes burns to the skin.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the microwave danger. Infrared is absorbed at the surface, so it burns the skin; microwaves pass in and heat tissue internally. Summer 2023 examiners named this pair as the common confusion.

context.setting: Two one-line facts that every electromagnetic wave shares

parts.stem: State what is true of the speeds of all seven regions of the electromagnetic spectrum when they travel through a vacuum.

accepted: they all travel at the same speed

scheme.for: they all travel at the same speed (3 × 10⁸ m/s)

hints: Wavelength and frequency change along the spectrum. Something does not.
parts.workedSolution: Every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed in a vacuum, 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Only the wavelength and the frequency change from one region to the next.

commonErrors.feedback: Different colours do travel at different speeds inside glass, which is why a prism makes a spectrum. In a vacuum every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed.

parts.stem: State whether electromagnetic waves are transverse or longitudinal.
hints: Only sound and ultrasound are in the other family.
parts.workedSolution: Transverse. Every electromagnetic wave is transverse, which is why they can travel through a vacuum with no particles to vibrate along.

emphasis: v = f lambda with the speed of light

context.setting: The microwaves inside a kitchen oven

parts.stem:
The microwaves inside a kitchen oven have a wavelength of 0.12 m. All electromagnetic waves travel at $3 \times 10^{8}$ m/s.
Calculate the frequency of these microwaves.

scheme.examinerNote: Physics papers print no equations, so the equation line is recalled and written before any number goes in; a number substituted into a wrong equation scores nothing.

hints: The same wave equation works for every electromagnetic wave; only the speed is fixed.
A short wavelength at that speed must give a very large frequency.
parts.workedSolution: v = f λ, so f = v ÷ λ. Substituting, 3 × 10⁸ = f × 0.12, so f = 3 × 10⁸ ÷ 0.12 = 2.5 × 10⁹ Hz.

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies the speed by the wavelength, which gives a speed times a length, not a frequency. Rearranging v = f λ for the frequency divides: f = v ÷ λ.
The division is upside down. The speed goes on top: f = v ÷ λ. A frequency smaller than one hertz for a microwave should look wrong immediately.

context.setting: A partly filled table of regions and their dangers

data.caption: Five regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, in order of increasing frequency.
rows: felt as heat; burns the skin
damages skin cells and can lead to skin cancer
damages cells, which may lead to cancer

parts.stem:
The table lists five regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency, with two names missing.
Name the missing region in the second row.
hints: It sits between microwaves and visible light.
Its danger is written beside it: burning the skin.
parts.workedSolution: Infrared. It lies between microwaves and visible light, and it is the one felt as heat.

parts.stem: Name the missing region in the fourth row.

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 examiners reported ultrasound written here instead of ultraviolet; ultrasound is a sound wave and is not on this table.

hints: It sits between visible light and X-rays.
Two words begin with ultra-. Only one of them is electromagnetic.
parts.workedSolution: Ultraviolet. It lies between visible light and X-rays, and it is the one that damages skin cells.

commonErrors.feedback: Ultrasound is sound, so it cannot be in the electromagnetic spectrum at all. The region between visible light and X-rays is ultraviolet. Summer 2025 examiners recorded this exact substitution on a Foundation table.

context.setting: A thermal imaging camera used by a vet to find inflammation

figures.alt: A thermal camera image of a dog. Its eyes, nose and the inside of its ears appear brightest on the screen, while the thick fur over its body appears much darker.

parts.stem:
A vet uses a thermal imaging camera, which builds a picture from the radiation an animal gives out.
Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum the camera detects.
hints: The picture is made from the warmth of the animal.
parts.workedSolution: Infrared. Warm objects give out infrared radiation, and a thermal camera turns the amount arriving from each point into a brightness on the screen.

parts.stem: State what the brightest parts of a thermal image have in common.

scheme.for: they are the hottest / warmest parts
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2024 examiners reported candidates who did not realise that hot objects emit infrared.

hints: Hotter objects emit more of this radiation.
parts.workedSolution: They are the hottest parts. The hotter an object is, the more infrared radiation it gives out, so those areas appear brightest.

commonErrors.feedback: Nothing in the picture is glowing with visible light. The brightness comes from infrared, and it is the hottest parts that emit the most of it. Summer 2024 examiners named this as a gap in the banded question on the spectrum.

parts.stem: Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum that lies between ultraviolet and gamma rays.
hints: It is the one used to photograph a broken bone.
parts.workedSolution: X-rays. Going up in frequency the last three regions are ultraviolet, X-rays and then gamma rays.

parts.stem: State what happens to the damage electromagnetic radiation can do to the body as its frequency increases.

scheme.for: the damage increases / it is more likely to cause damage

hints: Compare the danger of radio waves with the danger of gamma rays.
parts.workedSolution: The damage increases. The higher the frequency, the more damage the radiation is likely to do to the body, which is why gamma rays are far more dangerous than radio waves.

parts.stem:
A space probe near Saturn sends a radio signal and, at the same moment, a flash of visible light towards the Earth.
Explain why they reach the Earth at the same time.

accepted: all electromagnetic waves move through a vacuum at the same speed, and they cover the same distance

scheme.for: all electromagnetic waves move through a vacuum at the same speed (3 × 10⁸ m/s)
they travel the same distance, so they take the same time

hints: What do the two waves share, apart from their starting point?
parts.workedSolution: Every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed in a vacuum, 3 × 10⁸ m/s, whatever its frequency. Both signals cover the same distance through space, so both take the same time to arrive.

commonErrors.feedback: Neither is faster. Through a vacuum every electromagnetic wave moves at the same speed; only inside a material such as glass do different waves travel at different speeds.

context.setting: A poster for a school science corridor

parts.stem:
A class is making a poster about the electromagnetic spectrum for the science corridor.
Write an account of the spectrum for the poster. Name the seven regions in order, say what they all have in common, and give the harm that overexposure to three of them can do.
Your written communication is marked here as well: answer in full sentences, in a sensible order, using the specification's own scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: the seven regions in order: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
wavelength decreases and frequency increases along that order
every region moves through a vacuum at the same speed, 3 × 10⁸ m/s
microwaves cause internal heating of body tissues
infrared is felt as heat and burns the skin; intense visible light damages the eyes
ultraviolet damages skin cells and can cause skin cancer; X-rays and gamma rays damage cells, which may lead to cancer, and the higher the frequency the more damage

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Name the order first, then the two things they all share, then three dangers. That is seven points and five earn Band A.
Give each danger its own body part: internal tissue, skin, eyes, cells.
parts.workedSolution: The electromagnetic spectrum is a family of transverse waves. In order of increasing frequency the seven regions are radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays. Along that order the wavelength gets shorter and the frequency gets higher. In a vacuum every one of them travels at the same speed, 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Overexposure to any of them can be harmful, and the higher the frequency the more damage the radiation is likely to do. Microwaves cause internal heating of body tissues. Infrared is felt as heat and burns the skin, and intense visible light damages the eyes. Ultraviolet damages skin cells and can lead to skin cancer, while X-rays and gamma rays damage cells and may also lead to cancer.

commonErrors.feedback: The two ends of the spectrum are the wrong way round. Summer 2024 examiners named mixing up radio and gamma as the common error in this banded question. Radio waves have the lowest frequency and gamma rays the highest.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ciara is asked: 'Give one way in which overexposure to microwaves can harm the body. [1]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: Microwaves are used in ovens to cook food.
So microwaves are dangerous because they heat you up.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The idea of heating is right, but it stops one word short of the mark. Summer 2025 examiners credited heating only where it was linked to internal body tissue or organs: microwaves are absorbed by water inside you, so the heating happens under the skin. 'Heats you up' could equally describe infrared, which burns the surface instead.
correction: Microwaves are absorbed by water in the body.
They cause internal heating of body tissues.
That is the danger the specification names.
findTheMistake.feedback: No mark, and the fix is a single phrase. Where a danger is asked for, name the part of the body and the kind of harm: internal tissue for microwaves, the skin for infrared, skin cells for ultraviolet, the eyes for intense visible light, cells for X-rays and gamma rays.

prompts.prompt: Name the seven regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency.
prompts.answer: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

prompts.prompt: Which region of the spectrum has the longest wavelength?
What do all electromagnetic waves have in common, apart from being electromagnetic?
prompts.answer: They are all transverse, and they all move through a vacuum at the same speed: 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

prompts.prompt: Give the danger of overexposure to microwaves.
Give the danger of overexposure to ultraviolet.
prompts.answer: It damages skin cells and can lead to skin cancer.

prompts.prompt: How does the likely damage change as the frequency increases?
prompts.answer: The higher the frequency, the greater the damage it is likely to do.
